question.text: A limitation of VaR that the CVaR (Conditional VaR / Expected Shortfall) specifically addresses is:

answer.text: VaR is too easy to calculate
VaR does not describe the magnitude of losses BEYOND the VaR level
VaR is not used by regulators

explanation.text: The Logic: VaR reports a threshold loss at a given confidence level (e.g. 'the loss will not exceed Rs. X with 95% probability') but tells you nothing about how bad losses can get beyond that point. Conditional VaR / Expected Shortfall is designed to fill exactly that gap by averaging losses across the tail beyond the VaR cut-off, so it directly addresses VaR's silence on tail severity. The Trap: 'Too easy to calculate' is not a meaningful limitation; needing historical data is shared by most empirical risk measures, and CVaR does not solve that; the claim that VaR is not used by regulators is factually incorrect — VaR is one of the most widely used regulatory risk measures. Note: The NISM-Series-XXI-B workbook pages checked (pp. 289-292, 296-298 and 300) describe VaR as a loss threshold / lower-percentile metric but do not define Conditional VaR / Expected Shortfall in the pages checked; the only 'CVaR' usage there is Credit VaR (p. 297). The framing above is general industry/regulatory knowledge.
